chapters.title: Newtonian Dynamics & Momentum

Circular Dynamics and Centripetal Force

sections.heading: 1. The Fundamental Framework of Newton's Laws
sections.content:
Sir Isaac Newton formulated the three fundamental laws of motion in his 1687 treatise *Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica*. The first law, commonly known as the law of inertia, establishes that an isolated system experiences zero acceleration unless acted upon by a net external force.

Mathematically, \(\sum \vec{F} = 0 \implies \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = 0\). Inertia is directly proportional to inertial mass, representing the intrinsic resistance of matter to alterations in its state of rest or uniform rectilinear motion.

sections.heading: 2. Second Law: Force as Rate of Change of Momentum
sections.content:
The second law defines force precisely: the instantaneous rate of change of linear momentum \(\vec{p}\) is proportional to the applied force. For invariant mass \(m\):

$$\vec{F}_{net} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \frac{d(m\vec{v})}{dt} = m\frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = m\vec{a}$$

Key Dimension: \([M^1 L^1 T^{-2}]\), SI Unit: Newton (\(1\text{ N} = 1\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2\)).

sections.heading: 3. Action-Reaction Pairs and Conservation of Momentum
sections.content:
Newton's third law asserts: *To every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction*. Critically, action and reaction forces act on **two different bodies**, which is why they never cancel each other out.

When external forces sum to zero (\(\sum \vec{F}_{ext} = 0\)), total system momentum is invariant:
$$m_1 \vec{u}_1 + m_2 \vec{u}_2 = m_1 \vec{v}_1 + m_2 \vec{v}_2$$
This principle governs rocket propulsion, ballistic pendulums, and particle collisions.

formulas.label: Linear Momentum
formulas.note: Vector quantity in direction of velocity

notes.summary: Mechanics revolves around Newton's 3 laws. Force produces acceleration; momentum is conserved in isolated systems. Friction opposes impending relative motion.
keyPoints: Inertia depends solely on mass, not velocity or volume.
Action and reaction forces occur simultaneously and act on distinct objects.
Frictional force \(f_s \le \mu_s N\); kinetic friction is typically lower than maximum static friction.
Apparent weight in an elevator accelerating upward is \(N = m(g + a)\); accelerating downward is \(N = m(g - a)\).
notes.examTips: Always draw a Free Body Diagram (FBD) first! Resolve forces along parallel and perpendicular axes of motion before applying \(F = ma\).

book.title: Cosmic Mechanics and Gravitational Fields - Chapter 5
book.author: Dr. Carl Sagan & J. Kepler

sections.heading: 1. Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
sections.content:
Every particle attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers:

$$F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$$

Where \(G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2\) is the universal gravitational constant, verified experimentally by Henry Cavendish.

sections.heading: 2. Escape Velocity
sections.content:
Escape velocity is the minimum launch speed required for an unpowered projectile to overcome the gravitational binding energy of a celestial body without further propulsion:

$$v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR}$$

For Earth (\(R \approx 6.4 \times 10^6\text{ m}\)), \(v_e \approx 11.2\text{ km/s}\).

formulas.label: Kepler's 3rd Law
formulas.note: Orbital period squared is proportional to semi-major axis cubed

notes.summary: Gravitation is an attractive inverse-square central force. Escape velocity on Earth is 11.2 km/s. Kepler's third law connects orbital period to radius.
keyPoints: Value of \(g\) decreases both with height (\(g_h = g(1 - 2h/R)\)) and depth (\(g_d = g(1 - d/R)\)).
At the center of the Earth, \(g = 0\).
Geostationary satellites have an orbital time period of 24 hours at an altitude of approx 36,000 km.
notes.examTips: Remember that escape velocity is independent of the mass of the projectile! A feather and a rocket have the same escape velocity from Earth.

chapters.title: Electric Charges, Fields & Gauss's Law

Equipotential Surfaces and Capacitance

sections.heading: 1. Coulomb's Law and Electrostatic Force
sections.content:
The electrostatic force between two stationary point charges \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) separated by distance \(r\) in vacuum is:

$$F = \frac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_0} \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}$$

Where \(\epsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^2/(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2)\) is the permittivity of free space.

sections.heading: 2. Gauss's Law
sections.content:
The total electric flux \(\Phi_E\) passing through any closed Gaussian surface equals the net charge enclosed divided by \(\epsilon_0\):

$$\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{Q_{enclosed}}{\epsilon_0}$$

Gauss's law simplifies field calculation for symmetrical configurations (spherical, cylindrical, planar).

notes.summary: Coulomb's law dictates electrostatic forces. Gauss's law equates enclosed charge to total electric flux.
keyPoints: Electric field inside a hollow charged conductor is always zero.
Electric field lines never cross each other.
Dielectric of constant \(K\) placed between capacitor plates increases capacitance by factor \(K\).
notes.examTips: When choosing a Gaussian surface, ensure \(E\) is either parallel or perpendicular to \(dA\) for easy dot product integration.

syllabusTopics: L'Hôpital's Rule and Standard Limit Forms

Applications: Tangents, Normals, and Maxima/Minima

sections.heading: 1. Definition of the Derivative
sections.content:
The derivative of a real function \(f(x)\) measures the sensitivity to change of the function value with respect to a change in its argument. By the first principle:

$$f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$

Geometrically, it represents the instantaneous slope of the tangent line to the curve at coordinate \((x, f(x))\).

sections.heading: 2. Rules of Differentiation
sections.content:
- **Product Rule**: \((u \cdot v)' = u'v + uv'\)
- **Quotient Rule**: \(\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)' = \frac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}\)
- **Chain Rule**: \(\frac{d}{dx}[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)\)

notes.summary: Derivatives represent rate of change and slope. Critical points occur where \(f'(x) = 0\); second derivative test determines concavity and extrema.
keyPoints: If \(f'(c) = 0\) and \(f''(c) < 0\), \(x = c\) is a local maximum.
If \(f'(c) = 0\) and \(f''(c) > 0\), \(x = c\) is a local minimum.
Differentiability strictly implies continuity, but continuity does NOT guarantee differentiability (e.g., \(|x|\) at \(x=0\)).
notes.examTips: Always check for indeterminate forms before applying L'Hôpital's Rule. Differentiate numerator and denominator separately, NOT as a quotient rule!

sections.heading: 1. Asymptotic Complexity and Big-O Notation
sections.content:
Big-O notation describes the upper bound limiting behavior of a function when the argument tends towards a particular value or infinity. It quantifies worst-case time or memory consumption:

- \(O(1)\): Constant time (Hash table lookup, array indexing)
- \(O(\log N)\): Logarithmic time (Binary search)
- \(O(N)\): Linear time (Linear scan)
- \(O(N \log N)\): Linearithmic time (Merge sort, Heap sort)
- \(O(N^2)\): Quadratic time (Bubble sort, Selection sort)

sections.heading: 2. Stacks: Last-In, First-Out (LIFO)
sections.content:
A Stack is a linear data structure following the LIFO principle. Key operations include:

- `push(element)`: Appends to top of stack - \(O(1)\)
- `pop()`: Removes topmost element - \(O(1)\)
- `peek()`: Inspects topmost element without deletion - \(O(1)\)

Applications: Recursion call stacks, syntax parsing, bracket matching, undo/redo mechanisms.

notes.summary: Big-O evaluates algorithm scalability. Stacks operate on LIFO; Queues operate on FIFO.
keyPoints: Binary search requires a sorted array; time complexity is \(O(\log N)\).
Stack overflow occurs when pushing to a full stack; stack underflow happens when popping an empty stack.
Circular queue avoids memory wastage encountered in basic linear array-based queues.
notes.examTips: Be prepared to convert infix expressions to postfix using an operator stack and step-by-step trace tables.

sections.heading: 1. VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry
sections.content:
VSEPR postulates that electron pairs in the valence shell of a central atom repel each other and orient themselves to minimize electrostatic repulsion. The order of repulsive forces is:

$$\text{Lone Pair - Lone Pair} > \text{Lone Pair - Bond Pair} > \text{Bond Pair - Bond Pair}$$

Hence, \(\text{CH}_4\) has tetrahedral geometry (109.5°), \(\text{NH}_3\) is trigonal pyramidal (107°), and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) has a bent structure (104.5°).

formulas.label: Bond Order
formulas.note: Nb: bonding electrons, Na: antibonding electrons

formulas.label: Formal Charge
formulas.note: V: valence, L: lone pair e-, B: bond pair e-

notes.summary: Repulsion between valence electrons dictates geometry. Bond order \(> 0\) signifies stable molecular existence.
keyPoints: Water has \(sp^3\) hybridization with 2 lone pairs giving a bent shape of 104.5°.
If bond order is 0, the diatomic molecule does not exist (e.g. \(\text{He}_2\)).
Molecules with unpaired electrons in molecular orbitals are paramagnetic (e.g. \(\text{O}_2\)).
notes.examTips: Remember oxygen (\(\text{O}_2\)) is paramagnetic despite having an even number of electrons—MOT proves this with 2 unpaired electrons in \(\pi^*\) orbitals!

sections.heading: 1. Photosynthesis Equation & Mechanism
sections.content:
Photosynthesis is the biochemical pathway converting solar photons into chemical bond energy stored in glucose:

$$6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{h\nu, \text{chlorophyll}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2$$

It takes place in chloroplasts in two phases: the light-dependent reactions in thylakoids yielding ATP and NADPH, and the Calvin cycle in the stroma fixing \(\text{CO}_2\).

notes.summary: Chloroplasts synthesize glucose; mitochondria synthesize ATP via cellular respiration. DNA is a double helix held by hydrogen bonds.
keyPoints: Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) is the universal energy currency of cells.
In DNA, Adenine pairs with Thymine (2 H-bonds) and Guanine pairs with Cytosine (3 H-bonds).
Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces ethanol and \(\text{CO}_2\); in human muscle cells it produces lactic acid.
notes.examTips: Watch out for question phrasing on gas exchange: plants produce oxygen during the day via photosynthesis, but respire consuming oxygen continuously 24/7!
